Prediction-Powered Data Fusion for Treatment Effect Estimation

Yonghan Jung1 and Shu Yang2
1 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    yonghan@illinois.edu
2 North Carolina State University    syang24@ncsu.edu
October 23, 2026
Abstract

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) identify treatment effects without confounding but are often small, whereas observational studies (OBS) are large but may be confounded. Many estimators combining a small RCT with a large OBS have been developed for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the conditional ATE (CATE). However, existing ATE estimators either make assumptions on the OBS or do not borrow enough power from them. The CATE has been studied less than the ATE. Existing CATE methods either assume the OBS are unconfounded, rely on a model of the confounding function, or accept bias in exchange for lower variance. We therefore propose a framework that, without special assumptions on the OBS, fuses the OBS and the RCT by preserving the unbiasedness of RCT-based estimation while borrowing power from the large OBS to boost precision. Applying this principle, we build an ATE estimator, AIPW-Fusion, with closed-form weights and confidence intervals, and two CATE learners, DR-Fusion and R-Fusion. Experiments corroborate our findings.

1 Introduction

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for identifying treatment effects but are often small, whereas observational studies (OBS) are large but may be confounded. This paper fuses the two to estimate the trial-population conditional and average treatment effects.

Transportability and data-fusion methods (Bareinboim and Pearl, 2016; Colnet et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2023b; Jung et al., 2023a; Lee et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2024) identify and estimate effects that no single source identifies, such as effects in a new target population or of joint treatments. Most of them do not address cases where the RCT already identifies the target but is too small to estimate it precisely. Our work is closer to robust borrowing methods. For the ATE, they improve a trial estimate by combining it with OBS estimates or OBS-based predictions (Yang and Ding, 2020; Rosenman et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025; Gagnon-Bartsch et al., 2023; De Bartolomeis et al., 2025), or by prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Angelopoulos et al., 2026; Demirel et al., 2024, PPI;). Compared with ATE fusion, only a few fusion methods have been developed for CATE estimation, which use the trial to correct the bias of OBS-based estimates or the OBS to reduce the variance of trial-based ones (Kallus et al., 2018; Cheng and Cai, 2021; Wu and Yang, 2022; Li et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Hatt et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2023; Asiaee et al., 2025). Section 1.1 compares them with ours.

In this paper, we enhance treatment effect estimators from a small RCT with large, potentially heavily confounded OBS data while keeping them unbiased. Specifically, our contributions are:

  1. (i)

    An ATE estimator, AIPW-Fusion (AIPWF), that stays unbiased under any OBS confounding and combines two approaches, leveraging the OBS regressions plugged into the RCT’s AIPW score and a PPI correction, with a valid interval under an estimated ratio (Sec. 3).

  2. (ii)

    Two CATE learners, DR-Fusion (DRF) and R-Fusion (RF), that keep the trial’s CATE target under any OBS confounding, borrow without modeling the confounding function, and whose data-driven borrowing provably does almost no worse than the trial alone (Sec. 4).

  3. (iii)

    Experiments on synthetic data and the IHDP and ACIC 2016 benchmarks, where our estimators outperform trial-only estimation, PPI, and naive pooling (Sec. 5).

Code is available at https://github.com/CausalDataScience/DataFusionPPI.

Section 2 sets up the problem. Sections 3 and 4 develop the ATE estimator and the CATE learners. Section 5 reports the experiments. The appendix contains the proofs and additional results.

1.1 Related Work

Transportability.

Transportability and data-fusion methods (Pearl and Bareinboim, 2011; Bareinboim and Pearl, 2012; Pearl and Bareinboim, 2014; Bareinboim and Pearl, 2016; Lee et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022; Jung et al., 2023b; Jung et al., 2023a; Jung et al., 2024) combine sources to identify effects that no single source identifies, as reviewed by Colnet et al. (2024) and Shi et al. (2023). We instead borrow from the OBS to estimate more efficiently an effect that the trial already identifies.

Causal online learning.

Zhang and Bareinboim (2017) bound the expected reward of each arm from confounded observational data and clip the arm’s upper confidence bound at these bounds. Bareinboim (2025, Sec. 9.2) develops this as causal offline-to-online learning (COOL) (see also Bareinboim et al., 2025, Sec. 5). The clipping helps only while the experimental bound is looser than the causal bounds, and it assumes one population; we let the OBS differ from the trial in both the covariate law and the outcome regression (Assumption 3(ii)).

ATE fusion.

Table 1 compares the ATE fusion methods. Methods that put OBS outcomes directly into the estimate are not unbiased under every OBS confounding (Yang and Ding, 2020; Rosenman et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025). van der Laan et al. (2026) also pool the OBS outcomes but subtract an estimate of the OBS bias, so their estimator is consistent, though not unbiased, under any OBS confounding. Other methods add a prediction from external data as a covariate in the trial’s estimator (Gagnon-Bartsch et al., 2023; De Bartolomeis et al., 2025). A common choice is the prognostic score, each participant’s predicted outcome under control from a model trained on historical data (Schuler et al., 2022; Liao et al., 2025; Højbjerre-Frandsen et al., 2026). As in standard covariate adjustment in trials (Moore and van der Laan, 2009; Rosenblum and van der Laan, 2010; Moore et al., 2011), randomization keeps these estimators unbiased under any OBS confounding. Two methods instead generalize the trial ATE to a different target population: Lee et al. (2023) weight the trial to match the target’s covariates, and Demirel et al. (2024) apply PPI (Angelopoulos et al., 2023) by averaging predictions over the target covariates. van der Laan and van der Laan (2026) show that PPI and PPI++ are AIPW estimators, the latter with empirical efficiency maximization (Rubin and van der Laan, 2008). AIPWF combines the two channels of the methods above, putting OBS regressions into the trial’s AIPW score and a PPI correction over the OBS covariates, with coefficients chosen jointly in closed form (Sec. 3); Appendix B.4 compares it with prognostic-score adjustment.

CATE fusion.

Table 2 compares the CATE fusion methods. Existing methods keep the trial’s target only if the OBS are unconfounded (Li et al., 2022), only if the OBS bias follows a parametric, confounding-function, or representation model (Kallus et al., 2018; Wu and Yang, 2022; Yang et al., 2025; Hatt et al., 2022), or only up to a bias accepted for lower variance (Cheng and Cai, 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2023). Asiaee et al. (2025) keep this target under any OBS confounding by modeling the discrepancy between OBS predictions and trial outcome means. DRF and RF need no such model: they borrow through the two AIPWF channels inside orthogonal DR- and RR-learner losses (Sec. 4). Related work learns treatment rules for an observational target population (Wu and Yang, 2023) or estimates effects within strata of predicted risk (Kent et al., 2020).

2 Background and Setting

Fig. 1 describes the data-generating processes for RCT and OBS. Each unit has covariates X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, a binary treatment A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\}, and an outcome YY; PRP_{R} and POP_{O} denote the RCT and OBS distributions of V=(X,A,Y)V=(X,A,Y). In the RCT, treatment AA depends only on the covariates through a known propensity e⁡(x)e(x). In the OBS, an unmeasured confounder UU affects both treatment AA and outcome YY. With potential outcomes Y⁡(1)Y(1) and Y⁡(0)Y(0), the targets are the RCT-population conditional and average treatment effects τ0​(x)\tau_{0}(x) and θ0\theta_{0}. Tables 3 and 4 collect the notation.

Assumption 1 (Trial identification).

(i) Y=Y⁡(A)Y=Y(A) a.s.; (ii) {Y⁡(0),Y⁡(1)}⟂A|X\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp A\mid X under PRP_{R}; (iii) ee is known and bounded away from 00 and 11.

Each source S∈{R,O}S\in\{R,O\} is split into three i.i.d. samples from PSP_{S}: nuisance, tuning, and evaluation samples DSnuisD_{S}^{\mathrm{nuis}}, DStuneD_{S}^{\mathrm{tune}}, and DSevalD_{S}^{\mathrm{eval}} (Table 3). The three roles can be rotated across the samples and the resulting estimates averaged (cross-fitting), as in Sec. 5; our exact results are for a single split.

Assumption 2 (Sample separation).

The six samples DRnuisD_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}, DRtuneD_{R}^{\mathrm{tune}}, DRevalD_{R}^{\mathrm{eval}}, DOnuisD_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}, DOtuneD_{O}^{\mathrm{tune}}, and DOevalD_{O}^{\mathrm{eval}} are mutually independent.

All displayed moments are finite; stronger moment conditions are stated where needed.

We consider two settings for the covariate distributions PRXP_{R}^{X} and POXP_{O}^{X}: the RCT and OBS share the same domain, or they come from heterogeneous domains. In both, the OBS may be confounded. Whenever PRXP_{R}^{X} is absolutely continuous with respect to POXP_{O}^{X}, written PRX≪POXP_{R}^{X}\ll P_{O}^{X} (every covariate region with positive probability in the RCT also has positive probability in the OBS), the density ratio r0r_{0} exists.

Assumption 3 (Covariate domains).

One of the following holds.

  1. (i)

    (Same domain.) PRX=POXP_{R}^{X}=P_{O}^{X}, so r0≡1r_{0}\equiv 1.

  2. (ii)

    (Heterogeneous domains.) PRX≪POXP_{R}^{X}\ll P_{O}^{X}, so r0r_{0} exists; it need not be known.

Lemma 1 (RCT-valid AIPW score).

For any fixed measurable q:𝒳×{0,1}→ℝq:\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}\to\mathbb{R}, the AIPW score, with ee evaluated at XX,

φ⁡(V,q)≜q⁡(X,1)−q⁡(X,0)+Ae​{Y−q⁡(X,1)}−1−A1−e​{Y−q⁡(X,0)}\varphi(V;q)\triangleq q(X,1)-q(X,0)+\tfrac{A}{e}\{Y-q(X,1)\}-\tfrac{1-A}{1-e}\{Y-q(X,0)\} (1)

satisfies 𝔼R​[φ⁡(V,q)∣X]=τ0​(X)\mathbb{E}_{R}[\varphi(V;q)\mid X]=\tau_{0}(X) under Assumption 1 (Appendix A).

Hence the RCT-only AIPW estimator ℙR,n​Z0\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{0} is conditionally unbiased for θ0\theta_{0} given DRnuisD_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}.

3 Fusion for the ATE

In this section, we build the ATE estimator, called AIPWF, that uses a small RCT sample and borrows power from possibly confounded OBS.

3.1 Estimator, Variance, and Oracles

Our estimator starts from Lemma 1: ℙR,n​Z0\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{0} is the RCT-only AIPW estimator, and ℙR,n​Zλ\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{\lambda} is also unbiased for any λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}; that is, we can use the blended regressor μ^λ\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda} (Table 3) rather than the RCT-only regressor μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} to borrow power from the OBS (Gagnon-Bartsch et al., 2023; De Bartolomeis et al., 2025). Augmenting ℙR,n​Zλ\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{\lambda} with the PPI correction (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Angelopoulos et al., 2026), we define the AIPWF estimator:

Definition 1 (AIPWF estimator).

For fixed r:𝒳→[0,∞)r:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty) and (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega), the AIPWF estimator of θ0\theta_{0} is

θ^r​(λ,ω)≜ℙR,n​Zλ+ω⁡{ℙO,N​(r​g^)−ℙR,n​g^},\widehat{\theta}_{r}(\lambda,\omega)\triangleq\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{\lambda}+\omega\{\mathbb{P}_{O,N}(r\widehat{g})-\mathbb{P}_{R,n}\widehat{g}\}, (2)

with rr and g^\widehat{g} evaluated at XX. Equivalently, θ^r​(λ,ω)\widehat{\theta}_{r}(\lambda,\omega) is a sum of two independent sample means, an RCT term and an OBS term:

θ^r​(λ,ω)=ℙR,n​(Zλ−ω​g^)+ℙO,N​(ω​r​g^).\widehat{\theta}_{r}(\lambda,\omega)=\mathbb{P}_{R,n}(Z^{\lambda}-\omega\widehat{g})+\mathbb{P}_{O,N}(\omega r\widehat{g}). (3)

At (λ,ω)=(0,0)(\lambda,\omega)=(0,0) this is the RCT-only AIPW estimator ℙR,n​Z0\mathbb{P}_{R,n}Z^{0} (Robins et al., 1994). The coefficient λ\lambda sets the blended regressor μ^λ\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda} in the AIPW score, and ω\omega scales a transported control variate built from g^\widehat{g} (Fig. 2(a)). In this subsection, the density ratio is exact, r=r0r=r_{0}; Sec. 3.2 estimates it.

3.2 Estimating the Density Ratio

So far we have assumed r=r0r=r_{0}. This subsection gives the density-ratio estimator used in AIPWF. AIPWF is unbiased under the correct ratio (Thm. 1), but a misspecified ratio introduces bias.

Proposition 1 (Drift under a candidate ratio).

For a candidate ratio r~\widetilde{r}, let

𝚒𝚖𝚋f​(r~)≜𝔼O​[r~​f]−𝔼R​[f]=𝔼O​[(r~−r0)​f]\displaystyle\mathtt{imb}_{f}(\widetilde{r})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{O}[\widetilde{r}f]-\mathbb{E}_{R}[f]=\mathbb{E}_{O}[(\widetilde{r}-r_{0})f] (7)

be its imbalance along a feature ff. Then, for fixed (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega) and given the fitted regressions μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} and μ^O\widehat{\mu}_{O},

𝔼⁡[θ^r~​(λ,ω)]−θ0=ω​𝚒𝚖𝚋g^​(r~).\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\theta}_{\widetilde{r}}(\lambda,\omega)]-\theta_{0}=\omega\,\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}}(\widetilde{r}). (8)

Under Assumption 3(i) we set r^≡1\widehat{r}\equiv 1. Under Assumption 3(ii) the ratio must be estimated, and two characterizations of r0r_{0} give the estimators.

Proposition 2 (Characterizations of r0r_{0}).

Under Assumption 3(ii):

  1. (i)

    (Reweighting.) 𝔼O​[r0​h]=𝔼R​[h]\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}h]=\mathbb{E}_{R}[h] for every h∈L1​(PRX)h\in L^{1}(P_{R}^{X}), and no other weight does so for all bounded hh.

  2. (ii)

    (Riesz risk.) If r0∈L2​(POX)r_{0}\in L^{2}(P_{O}^{X}), then r0=arg⁡mina∈L2​(POX)​{𝔼O​[a2]−2​𝔼R​[a]}r_{0}=\arg\min_{a\in L^{2}(P_{O}^{X})}\{\mathbb{E}_{O}[a^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{R}[a]\}.

Item (ii) follows from item (i), since 𝔼O​[a2]−2​𝔼R​[a]=𝔼O​[(a−r0)2]−𝔼O​[r02]\mathbb{E}_{O}[a^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{R}[a]=\mathbb{E}_{O}[(a-r_{0})^{2}]-\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}^{2}]. Two base ratios are standard. The Riesz estimator r^RZ\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{RZ}} minimizes the empirical Riesz risk ℙOnuis​(a2)−2​ℙRnuis​(a)\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(a^{2})-2\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(a) of Prop. 2(ii) over a linear class (Chernozhukov et al., 2022), with a ridge penalty. The classifier estimator is r^CLS≜{(1−π^)/π^}​s^/(1−s^)\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CLS}}\triangleq\{(1-\widehat{\pi})/\widehat{\pi}\}\,\widehat{s}/(1-\widehat{s}), where s^​(x)\widehat{s}(x) is a fitted probability of trial membership given covariates xx, trained on the pooled nuisance covariates, and π^\widehat{\pi} is the trial share.

By Prop. 1, an estimated ratio biases AIPWF only through one moment, 𝚒𝚖𝚋g^​(r^)=𝔼O​[r^​g^]−𝔼R​[g^]\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{O}[\widehat{r}\widehat{g}]-\mathbb{E}_{R}[\widehat{g}]. A base ratio, such as r^RZ\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{RZ}} or r^CLS\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CLS}}, approximates r0r_{0} as a whole and leaves this moment nonzero in general. We therefore use calibration to achieve 𝔼O​[r^​g^]−𝔼R​[g^]=0\mathbb{E}_{O}[\widehat{r}\widehat{g}]-\mathbb{E}_{R}[\widehat{g}]=0.

Definition 2 (Calibrated balancing ratio).

Given a base ratio r^base>0\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}>0 and features f⁡(X)=(f1​(X),…,fK​(X))f(X)=(f_{1}(X),\dots,f_{K}(X)), the calibrated ratio is

r^BAL​(x)≜r^base​(x)​eξ^⊤​f​(x)ℙOnuis​{r^base​(X)​eξ^⊤​f​(X)},\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}}(x)\triangleq\frac{\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}(x)\,e^{\widehat{\xi}^{\top}f(x)}}{\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}\{\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}(X)e^{\widehat{\xi}^{\top}f(X)}\}},

Among ratios that average to one on the OBS and satisfy Eq. (9), r^BAL\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}} is the closest to r^base\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}} in Kullback–Leibler divergence (Hainmueller, 2012). For AIPWF, f=g^f=\widehat{g} suffices and is balanced exactly. Fig. 2(c) illustrates it: calibration drives each feature’s imbalance to zero, or within its tolerance δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k}.

Computing the calibrated ratio.

Eq. (9) is the stationarity condition of the convex objective log⁡ℙOnuis​{r^base​eξ⊤​f}−ξ⊤​ℙRnuis​(f)\log\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}\{\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}e^{\xi^{\top}f}\}-\xi^{\top}\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f), whose minimizer gives the Kullback–Leibler projection of r^base\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}} onto the ratios that satisfy Eq. (9) and average to one. For one feature, the stationarity condition says that the calibrated OBS mean of ff equals ℙRnuis​(f)\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f); its derivative in ξ\xi is the calibrated variance, which is nonnegative, so the root is unique when ℙRnuis​(f)\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f) lies strictly inside the range of ff on DOnuisD_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}. With many features (Secs. 4.3 and 5), we add the penalty ∑kδ^k​|ξk|\sum_{k}\widehat{\delta}_{k}|\xi_{k}| (approximate balance). The features ff have no intercept, δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k} is the standard error of the kkth balance residual, estimated by δ^k2=Var^Onuis​(r^base​fk)/Nnuis+Var^Rnuis​(fk)/nnuis\widehat{\delta}_{k}^{2}=\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}f_{k})/N_{\mathrm{nuis}}+\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f_{k})/n_{\mathrm{nuis}} with sample variances on DSnuisD_{S}^{\mathrm{nuis}} of sizes nnuisn_{\mathrm{nuis}} and NnuisN_{\mathrm{nuis}}, and ξ^\widehat{\xi} minimizes the objective below. The penalized dual objective

log⁡ℙOnuis​{r^base​eξ⊤​f}−ξ⊤​ℙRnuis​(f)+∑kδ^k​|ξk|\displaystyle\log\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}\{\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{base}}e^{\xi^{\top}f}\}-\xi^{\top}\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f)+\sum_{k}\widehat{\delta}_{k}|\xi_{k}| (10)

is convex in ξ\xi. At a minimizer ξ^\widehat{\xi}, the subgradient condition is ℙOnuis​(r^BAL​fk)−ℙRnuis​(fk)+δ^k​ςk=0\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}}f_{k})-\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(f_{k})+\widehat{\delta}_{k}\varsigma_{k}=0 with ςk∈∂|ξ^k|\varsigma_{k}\in\partial|\widehat{\xi}_{k}|. Hence the kkth residual is at most δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k} in absolute value, with equality when ξ^k≠0\widehat{\xi}_{k}\neq 0. Normalization gives ℙOnuis​(r^BAL)=1\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}})=1.

3.3 Algorithm and Confidence Intervals

This subsection gives an algorithm for the AIPWF estimate and its confidence interval.

We restrict (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega) to [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}, which contains the RCT-only estimator at (0,0)(0,0) and caps the PPI correction at its full weight ω=1\omega=1; λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] keeps μ^λ\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda} a convex blend of μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} and μ^O\widehat{\mu}_{O}. Since Thm. 1 needs A,B>0A,B>0 for the oracle coefficients −C/A-C/A and D/BD/B, we also prespecify thresholds ϵA,ϵB>0\epsilon_{A},\epsilon_{B}>0 and require A^>ϵA\widehat{A}>\epsilon_{A} and B^>ϵB\widehat{B}>\epsilon_{B}.

λ^\displaystyle\widehat{\lambda} ≜Proj[0,1](−C^/A^) 1{A^>ϵA},\displaystyle{}\triangleq\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(-\widehat{C}/\widehat{A})\,\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{A}>\epsilon_{A}\},
ω^\displaystyle\widehat{\omega} ≜Proj[0,1](D^/(B^+B^cal)) 1{B^>ϵB}.\displaystyle{}\triangleq\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{D}/(\widehat{B}+\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{cal}}))\,\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{B}>\epsilon_{B}\}. (11)

Here B^cal≜n⁡{Var^Rnuis​(g^)/nnuis+Var^Onuis​(r^​g^)/Nnuis}\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{cal}}\triangleq n\{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(\widehat{g})/n_{\mathrm{nuis}}+\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}(\widehat{r}\widehat{g})/N_{\mathrm{nuis}}\}, or 00 if r^≡1\widehat{r}\equiv 1, is the calibration noise of Thm. 2(ii).

Algorithm 1 uses the three samples of Assumption 2 in turn: it fits the nuisances, with r^\widehat{r} calibrated by Def. 2 with g^\widehat{g} among the features; selects (λ^,ω^)(\widehat{\lambda},\widehat{\omega}) by Eq. (11) from tuning-sample analogues of A,B,C,DA,B,C,D in Thm. 1; and evaluates Eq. (2), adding V^cal\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{cal}} (Thm. 2) to V^\widehat{V}.

Remark 2 (Adaptive reuse).

Algorithm 1 selects (λ^,ω^)(\widehat{\lambda},\widehat{\omega}) on the tuning samples and evaluates θ^\widehat{\theta} on separate samples, because selecting and evaluating on the same samples can bias the estimate. Theorem 2 (Confidence interval of the ATE estimator).

Let θ^=θ^r^​(λ^,ω^)\widehat{\theta}=\widehat{\theta}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\lambda},\widehat{\omega}), let 𝚒𝚖𝚋g^\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}} be as in Prop. 1, and let

    limn→∞P⁡(θ0∈[θ^±z1−α/2​(V^+V^cal)1/2])=1−α.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}P\big(\theta_{0}\in[\widehat{\theta}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}(\widehat{V}+\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{cal}})^{1/2}]\big)=1-\alpha. (14)

Item (i) shows that r^\widehat{r} moves the mean only through the drift ω^​𝚒𝚖𝚋g^​(r^)\widehat{\omega}\,\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}}(\widehat{r}), while V^\widehat{V} stays unbiased for VnV_{n}. Calibration does not make the drift zero. Eq. (9) holds on the nuisance samples, so 𝚒𝚖𝚋g^​(r^)=(ℙRnuis−𝔼R)​g^−(ℙOnuis−𝔼O)​(r^​g^)\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}}(\widehat{r})=(\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{nuis}}-\mathbb{E}_{R})\widehat{g}-(\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{nuis}}-\mathbb{E}_{O})(\widehat{r}\widehat{g}), a difference of nuisance-sample averages. It has mean approximately zero and standard deviation of order nnuis−1/2n_{\mathrm{nuis}}^{-1/2}, the order of the standard error. Thus, with r^BAL\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}}, item (i) gives a nonzero bias ω^​𝚒𝚖𝚋g^​(r^)\widehat{\omega}\,\mathtt{imb}_{\widehat{g}}(\widehat{r}) given the nuisance samples. Averaged over the nuisance samples, this bias is zero to first order, so θ^\widehat{\theta} is unbiased to first order. Item (ii) therefore treats it as noise and adds its variance V^cal\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{cal}}. It follows from the Lyapunov central limit theorem (van der Vaart, 1998, Prop. 2.27) for the four independent nuisance and evaluation samples.

4 Fusion for the CATE

In this section, we develop two CATE learners that borrow from the OBS in the same two ways as AIPWF: DRF, built on the AIPW pseudo-outcome of the DR-learner (Kennedy, 2023), and RF, built on the RR-learner loss (Nie and Wager, 2021). Throughout this section, Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, either Assumption 3(i) (r0≡1r_{0}\equiv 1) or Assumption 3(ii) holds, and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], so the blended regressor μ^λ\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda} is a convex combination of μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} and μ^O\widehat{\mu}_{O} and 𝔼R​[Zλ∣X]=τ0​(X)\mathbb{E}_{R}[Z^{\lambda}\mid X]=\tau_{0}(X) (Lemma 1). Table 4 collects the CATE notation.

4.1 CATE Risks

For a prespecified class 𝒯⊆L2​(PRX)\mathcal{T}\subseteq L^{2}(P_{R}^{X}), the CATE risk of t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} is

ℛ0​(t)≜𝔼R​[{t⁡(X)−τ0​(X)}2].\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{0}(t)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{R}[\{t(X)-\tau_{0}(X)\}^{2}]. (15)

The risk ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} requires the unknown τ0\tau_{0}. We therefore define a computable proxy:

Definition 3 (DRF and RF proxy risks).

For learner 𝚖𝚍𝚕∈{DRF,RF}\mathtt{mdl}\in\{\mathrm{DRF},\mathrm{RF}\}, let

κDRF\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathrm{DRF}} ≜1,\displaystyle\triangleq 1, ZDRFλ\displaystyle Z_{\mathrm{DRF}}^{\lambda} ≜Zλ,\displaystyle\triangleq Z^{\lambda},
κRF\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathrm{RF}} ≜(A−e)2e⁡(1−e),\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{(A-e)^{2}}{e(1-e)}, ZRFλ\displaystyle Z_{\mathrm{RF}}^{\lambda} ≜Y−mλA−e.\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{Y-m_{\lambda}}{A-e}.

The proxy risk of learner 𝚖𝚍𝚕\mathtt{mdl} is

ℛ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ)≜𝔼R​[κ𝚖𝚍𝚕​{Z𝚖𝚍𝚕λ−t⁡(X)}2].\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{R}[\kappa_{\mathtt{mdl}}\{Z_{\mathtt{mdl}}^{\lambda}-t(X)\}^{2}]. (16)

With ℙStune\mathbb{P}_{S}^{\mathrm{tune}} the average over DStuneD_{S}^{\mathrm{tune}}, ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}, and a candidate weight rr, its empirical proxy risk is

ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ,ω,r)≜ℙRtune​[κ𝚖𝚍𝚕​{Z𝚖𝚍𝚕λ−t⁡(X)}2]+ω​ℙOtune​[r​(g^−t)2]−ω​ℙRtune​[κ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(g^−t)2].\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda,\omega,r)\triangleq\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{tune}}[\kappa_{\mathtt{mdl}}\{Z_{\mathtt{mdl}}^{\lambda}-t(X)\}^{2}]+\omega\,\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{tune}}[r(\widehat{g}-t)^{2}]-\omega\,\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{tune}}[\kappa_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\widehat{g}-t)^{2}]. (17)

DRF regresses the AIPW score ZDRFλ=ZλZ^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DRF}}=Z^{\lambda}, as in the DR-learner (Kennedy, 2023). RF is the RR-learner (Nie and Wager, 2021) with each squared residual divided by e⁡(1−e)e(1-e), since {Y−mλ−(A−e)​t}2=e⁡(1−e)​κRF​{ZRFλ−t}2\{Y-m_{\lambda}-(A-e)t\}^{2}=e(1-e)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{RF}}\{Z_{\mathrm{RF}}^{\lambda}-t\}^{2}.

When r=r0r=r_{0}, in expectation, each empirical risk equals ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} up to an additive constant that does not depend on tt, so the two have the same minimizer.

Theorem 3 (Exact CATE targets).

Fix ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}, t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, and rr. Let Q𝚖𝚍𝚕​(λ)≜ℛ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(τ0,λ)Q_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\lambda)\triangleq\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\tau_{0};\lambda) be the loss at the true CATE. Then for 𝚖𝚍𝚕∈{DRF,RF}\mathtt{mdl}\in\{\mathrm{DRF},\mathrm{RF}\},

𝔼⁡[ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ,ω,r)]=Q𝚖𝚍𝚕​(λ)+ℛ0​(t)+ω​𝔼O​[(r−r0)​(g^−t)2].\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda,\omega,r)]=Q_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\lambda)+\mathcal{R}_{0}(t)+\omega\mathbb{E}_{O}[(r-r_{0})(\widehat{g}-t)^{2}].

Here Q𝚖𝚍𝚕​(λ)Q_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\lambda) does not depend on tt, and the last term is zero if r=r0r=r_{0}. In particular, if r=r0r=r_{0},

arg⁡mint∈𝒯⁡𝔼⁡[ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ,ω,r0)]=arg⁡mint∈𝒯​ℛ0​(t)\displaystyle\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda,\omega,r_{0})]=\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{R}_{0}(t) (18)

for all (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega).

At r=r0r=r_{0}, borrowing from the OBS never shifts the target, and (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega) change only the variance of the fitted learner (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3). At r≠r0r\neq r_{0}, the last term can shift the minimizer when ω>0\omega>0. The shift does not depend on λ\lambda, and for linear sieves calibration reduces it to nuisance-sampling error (Sec. 4.3).

The proposed empirical risk ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}} is, in expectation, an orthogonal risk (Foster and Syrgkanis, 2023) with respect to the RCT regression μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R}.

Proposition 3 (Orthogonality of the learning equation).

For t,s∈𝒯t,s\in\mathcal{T} and any fixed rr, not necessarily r0r_{0}, let

Ψ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t)​[s;μ^R,μ^O,r]≜−12​Dt​𝔼​[ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ,ω,r)]​[s]\displaystyle\Psi_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t)[s;\widehat{\mu}_{R},\widehat{\mu}_{O},r]\triangleq-\tfrac{1}{2}D_{t}\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda,\omega,r)][s] (19)

Then, for every h:𝒳×{0,1}→ℝh:\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}\to\mathbb{R} and every hrh_{r} with 𝔼O​[hr]=0\mathbb{E}_{O}[h_{r}]=0, writing Δ​h≜h⁡(⋅,1)−h⁡(⋅,0)\Delta h\triangleq h(\cdot,1)-h(\cdot,0), the derivative of Ψ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t)​[s]\Psi_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t)[s] at ε=0\varepsilon=0 is

  1. (i)

    00 along μ^R+ε​h\widehat{\mu}_{R}+\varepsilon h;

  2. (ii)

    ω​𝔼O​[(r−r0)​Δ​h​s]\omega\mathbb{E}_{O}[(r-r_{0})\,\Delta h\,s] along μ^O+ε​h\widehat{\mu}_{O}+\varepsilon h;

  3. (iii)

    ω​𝔼O​[hr​s​(g^−t)]\omega\mathbb{E}_{O}[h_{r}\,s\,(\widehat{g}-t)] along r+ε​hrr+\varepsilon h_{r}.

Thus Ψ𝚖𝚍𝚕\Psi_{\mathtt{mdl}} is orthogonal to μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} for every rr, to μ^O\widehat{\mu}_{O} only at r=r0r=r_{0}, and to rr only if g^=t\widehat{g}=t.

This is the orthogonality of the AIPW score and the RR loss to their outcome regressions under a known propensity (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Kennedy, 2023; Nie and Wager, 2021). At t=τ0t=\tau_{0}, g^=t\widehat{g}=t requires no unmeasured confounding in the OBS. In practice, we set r=r^r=\widehat{r}, fitted on the nuisance samples by the classifier estimator r^CLS\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CLS}} (Sec. 3.2) or the calibrated ratio r^BAL\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}} (Def. 2).

4.2 Fitting and Selecting Coefficients

We now select the coefficients. We define a grid 𝒢={(λm,ωm)}m=1M⊆[0,1]2\mathcal{G}=\{(\lambda_{m},\omega_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M}\subseteq[0,1]^{2}, compute for each mm the minimizer of the empirical proxy risk in Eq. (17), and choose the (λm,ωm)(\lambda_{m},\omega_{m}) whose minimizer has the smallest estimated CATE risk (Def. 4).

We write

τ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(⋅,λ,ω)∈arg⁡mint∈𝒯​ℛ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(t,λ,ω,r^)\displaystyle\widehat{\tau}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\cdot;\lambda,\omega)\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(t;\lambda,\omega,\widehat{r}) (20)

for this minimizer, the fitted fusion learner, with ties broken by a fixed rule (e.g., the smallest 𝔼R​[t​(X)2]\mathbb{E}_{R}[t(X)^{2}]).

For grid point mm, write τ^m≜τ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(⋅,λm,ωm)\widehat{\tau}_{m}\triangleq\widehat{\tau}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\cdot;\lambda_{m},\omega_{m}). We pick the τ^m\widehat{\tau}_{m} with the smallest validation score, defined below.

Definition 4 (Validation score on a finite grid).

Let 𝒢⊆[0,1]2\mathcal{G}\subseteq[0,1]^{2} be a prespecified finite grid containing (0,0)(0,0). For m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M,

ℛ^val​(τ^m,ωm)≜ℙR,n​[{Z0−τ^m​(X)}2]+ωm​ℙO,N​[r^​(g^−τ^m)2]−ωm​ℙR,n​[(g^−τ^m)2],\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};\omega_{m})\triangleq\mathbb{P}_{R,n}[\{Z^{0}-\widehat{\tau}_{m}(X)\}^{2}]+\omega_{m}\,\mathbb{P}_{O,N}[\widehat{r}(\widehat{g}-\widehat{\tau}_{m})^{2}]-\omega_{m}\,\mathbb{P}_{R,n}[(\widehat{g}-\widehat{\tau}_{m})^{2}], (21)

and (λ^𝚖𝚍𝚕,ω^𝚖𝚍𝚕)≜(λm^,ωm^)(\widehat{\lambda}_{\mathtt{mdl}},\widehat{\omega}_{\mathtt{mdl}})\triangleq(\lambda_{\widehat{m}},\omega_{\widehat{m}}) with m^∈arg⁡minm​ℛ^val​(τ^m,ωm)\widehat{m}\in\arg\min_{m}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};\omega_{m}). The score depends on λm\lambda_{m} through τ^m\widehat{\tau}_{m}. That is, ℛ^val​(τ^m,ωm)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};\omega_{m}) is the DRF empirical proxy risk of Eq. (17) with λ=0\lambda=0 and r=r^r=\widehat{r}, evaluated at t=τ^mt=\widehat{\tau}_{m} on the evaluation samples.

Since ℛ^val​(τ^m,ωm)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};\omega_{m}) is the DRF proxy risk ℛ^DRF​(τ^m,0,ωm,r^)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{DRF}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};0,\omega_{m},\widehat{r}) evaluated at a candidate fitted on other samples, Thm. 3 applies with λ=0\lambda=0. When r^=r0\widehat{r}=r_{0}, conditional on the fitted objects,

𝔼⁡[ℛ^val​(τ^m,ωm)]=QDRF​(0)+ℛ0​(τ^m).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}}(\widehat{\tau}_{m};\omega_{m})]=Q_{\mathrm{DRF}}(0)+\mathcal{R}_{0}(\widehat{\tau}_{m}). (22)

The constant QDRF​(0)Q_{\mathrm{DRF}}(0) is the same for every mm, so the score ranks the candidates by CATE risk.

Since ℛ^val\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{val}} uses finite samples and r^\widehat{r}, its minimizer may miss the best candidate; Thm. 4 bounds this loss.

Theorem 4 (Validation guarantee).

Suppose |Z0||Z^{0}|, |g^||\widehat{g}|, and all τ^m\widehat{\tau}_{m} are bounded by BB, and 0≤r^≤r¯0\leq\widehat{r}\leq\bar{r}. Let

ϱ𝚖𝚍𝚕​(λ,ω)≜ω​𝔼O​[(r^−r0)​{g^−τ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(⋅,λ,ω)}2]\displaystyle\varrho_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\lambda,\omega)\triangleq\omega\mathbb{E}_{O}[(\widehat{r}-r_{0})\{\widehat{g}-\widehat{\tau}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\cdot;\lambda,\omega)\}^{2}] (23)

be the transport error of r^\widehat{r} in Eq. (21), which is zero when r^=r0\widehat{r}=r_{0}. Conditional on the nuisance and tuning samples, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha,

ℛ0​{τ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(⋅,λ^𝚖𝚍𝚕,ω^𝚖𝚍𝚕)}≤min(λ,ω)∈𝒢⁡ℛ0​{τ^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(⋅,λ,ω)}+2​εeval​(α)+2​max𝒢​|ϱ𝚖𝚍𝚕|,\mathcal{R}_{0}\{\widehat{\tau}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\cdot;\widehat{\lambda}_{\mathtt{mdl}},\widehat{\omega}_{\mathtt{mdl}})\}\leq\min_{(\lambda,\omega)\in\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{R}_{0}\{\widehat{\tau}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\cdot;\lambda,\omega)\}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}(\alpha)+2\max_{\mathcal{G}}|\varrho_{\mathtt{mdl}}|, (24)

where M≜|𝒢|M\triangleq|\mathcal{G}| and

εeval(α)≜2B22​log⁡(4​M/α)(2n−1/2+r¯N−1/2).\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}(\alpha)\triangleq 2B^{2}\sqrt{2\log(4M/\alpha)}\,(2n^{-1/2}+\bar{r}N^{-1/2}). (25)

That is, the risk of the selected learner exceeds the smallest risk on the grid by at most a sampling term of order n−1/2+N−1/2n^{-1/2}+N^{-1/2} and a term from the error in r^\widehat{r}. Since (0,0)∈𝒢(0,0)\in\mathcal{G}, when r^=r0\widehat{r}=r_{0} the selected learner is at most 2​εeval​(α)2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}(\alpha) worse than the RCT-only learner.

4.3 Linear Sieves: Risk and Calibration

We now analyze DRF and RF when 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a linear sieve (Newey, 1997; Chen, 2007).

Definition 5 (Linear-sieve fusion learner).

Let ζ:𝒳→ℝp\zeta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} be fixed before tuning (e.g., splines, random features, or a neural network11 1 A frozen neural representation trained on the nuisance samples: the network is fit on DSnuisD_{S}^{\mathrm{nuis}}, and its weights are held fixed during tuning.), and 𝒯ζ≜{ζ⊤​β:β∈ℝp}\mathcal{T}_{\zeta}\triangleq\{\zeta^{\top}\beta:\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\}. τp⋆≜ζ⊤​βp=arg⁡mint∈𝒯ζ​ℛ0​(t)\tau^{\star}_{p}\triangleq\zeta^{\top}\beta_{p}=\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\zeta}}\mathcal{R}_{0}(t)

is the best approximation of τ0\tau_{0} in the sieve class 𝒯ζ\mathcal{T}_{\zeta} of Def. 5. The estimator β^𝚖𝚍𝚕\widehat{\beta}_{\mathtt{mdl}} has a closed form.

Proposition 4 (Normal equation).

Let H^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(ω)≜(1−ω)​ℙRtune​(κ𝚖𝚍𝚕​ζ​ζ⊤)+ω​ℙOtune​(r^​ζ​ζ⊤)\widehat{H}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\omega)\triangleq(1-\omega)\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{tune}}(\kappa_{\mathtt{mdl}}\zeta\,\zeta^{\top})+\omega\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{tune}}(\widehat{r}\zeta\,\zeta^{\top}). {H^𝚖𝚍𝚕​(ω)+ρ​I}​β=ℙRtune​{κ𝚖𝚍𝚕​ζ​(Z𝚖𝚍𝚕λ−ω​g^)}+ω​ℙOtune​(r^​ζ​g^).\{\widehat{H}_{\mathtt{mdl}}(\omega)+\rho I\}\beta=\mathbb{P}_{R}^{\mathrm{tune}}\{\kappa_{\mathtt{mdl}}\zeta(Z^{\lambda}_{\mathtt{mdl}}-\omega\widehat{g})\}+\omega\,\mathbb{P}_{O}^{\mathrm{tune}}(\widehat{r}\zeta\widehat{g}). (27)

where 𝚋𝚒𝚊𝚜⁡(ω)\mathtt{bias}(\omega) is from Prop. 5, and

At r^=r0\widehat{r}=r_{0}, both imbalances vanish, so only the ridge part 𝚋𝚒𝚊𝚜=ρ2​‖(ΓR+ρ​I)−1​βp‖ΓR2\mathtt{bias}=\rho^{2}\|(\Gamma_{R}+\rho I)^{-1}\beta_{p}\|^{2}_{\Gamma_{R}} remains.

Proposition 6 (Calibration for ATE and sieve CATE).

Let r^\widehat{r} satisfy Eq. (9) on the nuisance samples up to the tolerances δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k}. Then, for each balanced feature fkf_{k},

and likewise for their linear combinations.

Hence, with a calibrated r^\widehat{r}, the ratio part of 𝚋𝚒𝚊𝚜⁡(ω)\mathtt{bias}(\omega) in Thm. 5 is of order nnuis−1+Nnuis−1n_{\mathrm{nuis}}^{-1}+N_{\mathrm{nuis}}^{-1} and no longer depends on how well the base ratio approximates r0r_{0}, and the transport error in Thm. 4 is of order nnuis−1/2+Nnuis−1/2n_{\mathrm{nuis}}^{-1/2}+N_{\mathrm{nuis}}^{-1/2}. The ATE needs one feature, while the sieve CATE needs 1+p+p⁡(p+1)/21+p+p(p+1)/2, because the ratio enters the CATE through a pp-vector and a p×pp\times p matrix rather than a scalar. For a general class 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the ratio enters through 𝔼O​[(r^−r0)​s​(g^−t)]\mathbb{E}_{O}[(\widehat{r}-r_{0})s(\widehat{g}-t)] for every direction s∈𝒯s\in\mathcal{T} (Prop. 3), which no finite ff removes. Exact balance on many features is fragile, so each gap need only be within its standard error δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k} (Sec. 3.2).

5 Experiments

5.1 Designs

We use one synthetic design and two semi-synthetic benchmarks, IHDP (Hill, 2011) and ACIC 2016 (Dorie et al., 2019). In each design, the trial randomizes the treatment, whereas an unmeasured confounder UU affects both the treatment and the outcome in the OBS. The OBS bias is large: in the synthetic design, its root mean square is 1.5 times the standard deviation of τ0​(X)\tau_{0}(X) in the trial. The benchmarks keep their real covariates and noiseless response surfaces, and we simulate the treatments and outcomes. The OBS covariate law either equals the trial law (r0=1r_{0}=1) or is tilted away from it, which lowers the effective OBS sample fraction 1/𝔼O​[r02]1/\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}^{2}] to 0.70 (weak shift) or 0.40 (strong shift). Appendix B.1 gives the full designs.

5.2 Estimators and Metrics

For the ATE, we compare AIPWF (Fusion) with trial-only AIPW (Robins et al., 1994); PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2026), which uses the PPI correction alone (λ=0\lambda=0); Shrinkage (Rosenman et al., 2023, after) and Pretest, which combine the trial-only ATE with the ATE of a naive pool of all rows; and the naive pool itself. For the CATE, we compare DRF and RF with the trial-only DR- and R-learners (RCT), their PPI++ versions (λ=0\lambda=0), the 2-step learner (Kallus et al., 2018, after), the integrative RR-learner (IR) of Wu and Yang (2022), and the naive pool. The trial has nn between 300 and 3,000 units, the OBS has N=15,000N=15{,}000 units, and every split-based method is cross-fitted over three trial blocks. Each setting has 1,000 replications. We report the ATE mean squared error (MSE) and the CATE risk 𝔼R​{τ^​(X)−τ0​(X)}2\mathbb{E}_{R}\{\hat{\tau}(X)-\tau_{0}(X)\}^{2} relative to the trial-only AIPW estimator and DR-learner, so a ratio below 1 means that the OBS help. Appendix B.1 gives the nuisance models, the tuning rules, and the implementation of each baseline.

5.3 Main Results

Fig. 4 shows each error relative to the trial-only estimator on a log scale, so a curve below 1 improves on the trial alone. Fusion has the smallest MSE in every design, covariate law, and trial size (columns 1–4). It is also robust to the size of the confounding (column 5): its error stays flat as the bias grows. DRF and RF have the smallest risk in every design, covariate law, and trial size. They stay below the trial-only risk at every bias. Tables 5 and 6 give the numbers.

ATE.

Across the 45 settings (three designs, three covariate laws, five trial sizes), the MSE of fusion is 0.40 to 1.00 of the trial-only MSE (Table 5). The gain is largest for small trials (0.47 to 0.60 at n=300n=300 in Fig. 4) and shrinks as the trial grows. PPI++ stays near the trial-only MSE, at 0.95 to 1.07, because the PPI correction can remove at most the share of effect heterogeneity in the score variance (Remark 1), which is 0.02 to 0.10 in these designs. Shrinkage and Pretest stay at or above the trial-only MSE, and the naive pool is 8.6 to 184 times worse, because its confounding bias does not shrink with nn. Appendix B.4 compares fusion with two prognostic-score adjustments (Schuler et al., 2022), which put the same OBS prediction into a trial regression: they are slightly better than fusion on IHDP at n=300n=300 under a shift but up to 1.5 times worse than the trial alone on the synthetic design, whereas fusion never exceeds the trial-only MSE. The Wald intervals of fusion have coverage 0.94 to 0.96 and are 63% to 99% as wide as the trial-only ones (Tables 14 and 15).

CATE.

DRF and RF have 0.53 to 0.67 of the trial-only risk in all 45 settings and differ from each other by at most 0.01 (Table 6). Their PPI++ versions catch up only at n=3,000n=3{,}000. Fitting the trial loss alone on the same sieve, which uses g^\widehat{g} only as a basis function, shows that at small nn most of the gain comes from the fusion loss and at large nn from g^\widehat{g} as a basis function (Appendix B.3). IR improves on the trial only on ACIC and on IHDP at n=300n=300, and 2-step stays at 0.90 to 1.30 in the settings of Fig. 4. Both model the OBS bias, so the OBS help them only when the bias follows that model.

Further results.

Appendix B.2 repeats the bias sweep of Fig. 4 at other trial sizes and varies the OBS size NN. Appendix B.3 separates the two channels λ\lambda and ω\omega, compares fusion with practitioner’s trial-only baselines, and studies a misspecified density ratio, where the calibrated ratio keeps fusion unbiased, and a design with larger effect heterogeneity, where ω\omega improves on λ\lambda alone when the covariate laws coincide.

6 Conclusion

For the ATE, AIPWF has closed-form optimal weights (Thm. 1, Cor. 1.1) and valid Wald intervals with a calibrated ratio (Thm. 2). For the CATE, DRF and RF keep the trial’s CATE risk as their target (Thm. 3), validation selects the weights with a guarantee relative to the RCT-only learner (Thm. 4), and for linear sieves, calibration on finitely many moments controls the ratio error in the risk (Thm. 5, Prop. 6). Fusion has the lowest ATE error, and DRF and RF the lowest CATE risk, among the estimators of Section 5 in every design and trial size. Prognostic-score adjustment is slightly better than fusion on one benchmark but up to 1.5 times worse than the trial alone on another, whereas fusion never exceeds the trial-only error (Appendix B.4).

Appendix A Proofs

Orthogonality.

Sec. 4 states which fitted nuisances enter the first-order condition of a loss. The following two definitions fix the language.

Definition 6 (Gateaux derivative (van der Vaart, 1998, Chapter 20)).

Let FF be a functional of a function-valued argument η\eta, and let hh be a direction such that η+ε​h\eta+\varepsilon h stays in the domain of FF for all sufficiently small |ε||\varepsilon|. Whenever the limit exists, the Gateaux derivative of FF at η\eta in the direction hh is

Dη​F​(η)​[h]\displaystyle D_{\eta}F(\eta)[h] ≜dd​ε​F​(η+ε​h)|ε=0\displaystyle\triangleq\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}F(\eta+\varepsilon h)\right|_{\varepsilon=0} (30)
Definition 7 (Learning equation and orthogonality (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Foster and Syrgkanis, 2023)).

Let L⁡(t,η)L(t;\eta) be a population loss with a target argument tt in a linear class and a nuisance argument η\eta, and let η0\eta_{0} denote the true nuisance. The learning equation of LL is

Ψ​(t,η)​[s]\displaystyle\Psi(t;\eta)[s] ≜−12​Dt​L​(t,η)​[s]\displaystyle\triangleq-\frac{1}{2}D_{t}L(t;\eta)[s] (31)

for target directions ss in the class. The loss is orthogonal to η\eta if Dη​Ψ​(t⋆,η0)​[h,s]=0D_{\eta}\Psi(t^{\star};\eta_{0})[h,s]=0 for every admissible nuisance direction hh and every target direction ss.

When LL is convex in tt, a function t⋆t^{\star} minimizes L⁡(⋅,η0)L(\cdot\,;\eta_{0}) over the class exactly when Ψ⁡(t⋆,η0)​[s]=0\Psi(t^{\star};\eta_{0})[s]=0 for every ss in the class, which is why Ψ\Psi is called the learning equation.

Appendix B Additional Simulation Results

Appendix B.1 gives the full experimental setup, Appendix B.2 the bias and observational-sample-size sweeps, Appendix B.3 the ablations and further designs, and Appendix B.4 the comparison with prognostic-score adjustment. Appendix B.5 gives the remaining results.

B.1 Experimental Details

A latent UU confounds the OBS in a synthetic design and two semi-synthetic benchmarks, IHDP (Hill, 2011) and ACIC 2016 (Dorie et al., 2019); the bias has root mean square 1.5​sdR​{τ0​(X)}1.5\,\mathrm{sd}_{R}\{\tau_{0}(X)\} in the synthetic design. The benchmarks keep only their real covariates and noiseless surfaces μ0,μ1\mu_{0},\mu_{1}, and both samples draw rows of this table. The trial randomizes AA, and the OBS assigns AA through XX and UU, which also enters Y=μA​(X)+U+εY=\mu_{A}(X)+U+\varepsilon. The OBS covariate law equals the trial law (r0=1r_{0}=1) or tilts it by exp⁡{a​h​(X)}\exp\{a\,h(X)\} for a standardized direction hh (the first principal component in the benchmarks), so r0∝exp⁡(−a​h)r_{0}\propto\exp(-a\,h).

Synthetic design.

The covariates are X=l​U+0.9​ϵX∈ℝ10X=lU+0.9\,\epsilon_{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{10} with U∼N⁡(0,1)U\sim N(0,1) and ϵX∼N⁡(0,I10)\epsilon_{X}\sim N(0,I_{10}), where ll loads UU on the first two coordinates with weights ±0.5\pm 0.5, so that Var⁡(U∣X)=0.62\mathrm{Var}(U\mid X)=0.62. The outcome is Y=m⁡(X)+2​U+A​τ​(X)+0.7​εY=m(X)+2U+A\tau(X)+0.7\varepsilon with ε∼N⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim N(0,1), where mm is a fixed combination of linear, sine, quadratic, and pairwise-product terms and τ\tau is a nonlinear function with 𝔼R​τ​(X)=0.8\mathbb{E}_{R}\tau(X)=0.8 and VarR​τ​(X)=1.47\mathrm{Var}_{R}\tau(X)=1.47. The trial sets A∼Bernoulli⁡(0.35)A\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.35). The OBS sets A∼Bernoulli⁡[clip⁡{expit⁡(η⁡(X)+ν⁡(X)​U),0.05,0.95}]A\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}[\mathrm{clip}\{\mathrm{expit}(\eta(X)+\nu(X)U),0.05,0.95\}] for a fixed index η\eta, with ν⁡(x)=ν0​{1+ηstd​(x)}\nu(x)=\nu_{0}\{1+\eta_{\mathrm{std}}(x)\} and ηstd\eta_{\mathrm{std}} the index standardized over the trial covariates, so the confounding is strongest for units that are likely to be treated. The bias of the OBS contrast is δ(x)=2{𝔼O[U∣A=1,X=x]−𝔼O[U∣A=0,X=x]}\delta(x)=2\{\mathbb{E}_{O}[U\mid A=1,X=x]-\mathbb{E}_{O}[U\mid A=0,X=x]\}, computed by Gauss–Hermite quadrature, and ν0\nu_{0} sets {𝔼R​δ​(X)2}1/2=1.5​sdR​{τ0​(X)}\{\mathbb{E}_{R}\delta(X)^{2}\}^{1/2}=1.5\,\mathrm{sd}_{R}\{\tau_{0}(X)\}. The bias sweep changes only ν0\nu_{0} so that this root mean square is 0,0.25,…,1.250,0.25,\dots,1.25 times sdR​{τ0​(X)}\mathrm{sd}_{R}\{\tau_{0}(X)\}.

Benchmarks.

IHDP (Hill, 2011) has 747 units, 25 covariates, and 100 realizations of its response surfaces in the release that accompanies Shalit et al. (2017). ACIC 2016 (Dorie et al., 2019) has 4,802 units and 58 covariates, three of them categorical and one-hot encoded, and we use its settings 1–10. We discard the treatments and outcomes recorded in both data sets and keep only the covariates and the noiseless surfaces. Both samples draw rows of the covariate table with replacement. The benchmarks are thus finite-population designs. An OBS sample of 15,000 rows contains each IHDP row about 20 times on average and each ACIC row about 3 times, and a trial of n=3,000n=3{,}000 contains each IHDP row about 4 times. The CATE risk averages over the rows of the table (Metrics), so it is computed at covariate values that also appear in the OBS sample, and the repeated rows may make the OBS regression more accurate there than it would be at new covariate values. Replication kk uses IHDP realization kmod100k\bmod 100 and ACIC setting (kmod10)+1(k\bmod 10)+1. The published noiseless surfaces μ0,μ1\mu_{0},\mu_{1} are scaled so that VarR​μA​(X)=1\mathrm{Var}_{R}\mu_{A}(X)=1, and Y=μA​(X)+U+εY=\mu_{A}(X)+U+\varepsilon with U,ε∼N⁡(0,1)U,\varepsilon\sim N(0,1) independent of XX. The trial draws rows uniformly and sets A∼Bernoulli⁡(0.35)A\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.35). The OBS treatment follows the rule of the synthetic design with η\eta linear in three standardized covariates, and ν0\nu_{0} sets |𝔼R​δ​(X)|=0.50​sdR​(Y)|\mathbb{E}_{R}\delta(X)|=0.50\,\mathrm{sd}_{R}(Y), where δ(x)=𝔼O[U∣A=1,X=x]−𝔼O[U∣A=0,X=x]\delta(x)=\mathbb{E}_{O}[U\mid A=1,X=x]-\mathbb{E}_{O}[U\mid A=0,X=x].

Covariate shift.

A shift changes the law of XX only, not that of (U,A,Y)(U,A,Y) given XX. In the synthetic design, the OBS covariates have mean a​da\,d instead of zero for a fixed direction dd, which is the exponential tilt exp⁡(a​d⊤​Σ−1​x)\exp(a\,d^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x) with Σ=Cov⁡(X)\Sigma=\mathrm{Cov}(X). In the benchmarks, the OBS draws row ii with probability proportional to exp⁡(a​hi)\exp(ah_{i}), where hh is the standardized first principal component of the standardized covariates. Since the trial draws rows uniformly, the density ratio at row ii is r0​(xi)=ea​h¯/ea​hir_{0}(x_{i})=\overline{e^{ah}}/e^{ah_{i}}, where ea​h¯\overline{e^{ah}} is the average of ea​hje^{ah_{j}} over the rows, and 1/𝔼O​[r02]=1/(ea​h¯​e−a​h¯)1/\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}^{2}]=1/(\overline{e^{ah}}\,\overline{e^{-ah}}). In the synthetic design, with h⁡(x)=d⊤​Σ−1​xh(x)=d^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x and d⊤​Σ−1​d=1d^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}d=1, r0​(x)=exp⁡{a2/2−a​h​(x)}r_{0}(x)=\exp\{a^{2}/2-a\,h(x)\} and 1/𝔼O​[r02]=e−a21/\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}^{2}]=e^{-a^{2}}. The constant aa sets the effective sample fraction 1/𝔼O​[r02]1/\mathbb{E}_{O}[r_{0}^{2}] to 0.400.40 (the shift of Fig. 4) or 0.700.70 (the weak shift of Tables 5 and 6).

Samples and estimators.

A trial of size nn is split into equal nuisance, tuning, and evaluation samples, and the OBS has N=15,000N=15{,}000 rows split 60/20/2060/20/20; Fig. 6 varies NN. Every split-based method is cross-fitted: the three trial roles rotate over three equal blocks, each method runs once per rotation, and the three ATE estimates or CATE predictions are averaged. The naive pool instead fits one regression on all trial and OBS rows, and Shrinkage and Pretest combine it with the cross-fitted trial-only estimate. The OBS keeps one split because it is large. Here nn and NN are the total trial and OBS sizes, so the evaluation sizes in each rotation, written nn and NN in Secs. 3 and 4, are n/3n/3 and 0.2​N0.2N. Thm. 2 applies to each rotation. The Wald interval of the averaged ATE uses a first-order standard error of the average: each trial unit contributes its score Zλ^−ω^​g^Z^{\widehat{\lambda}}-\widehat{\omega}\widehat{g} from the rotation that evaluates its block and, with an estimated ratio, the calibration term ω^​g^​(X)\widehat{\omega}\widehat{g}(X) from the rotation whose nuisance sample contains it, and the OBS adds the variances of its rotation-averaged evaluation scores and calibration terms ω^​r^​g^\widehat{\omega}\widehat{r}\widehat{g}. The same OBS random numbers are used under every covariate law. Both outcome regressions are ridge regressions (penalty 5) of YY on (f,A,A​f)(f,A,Af), where ff standardizes XX, X2X^{2}, sin⁡X\sin X, and the pairwise products of the first six covariates, and their predictions are clipped to the 0.5% to 99.5% range of each arm on the fitting sample. Z1,…,Z5Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5} are the first five principal components of the standardized trial nuisance covariates, scaled to unit variance. When r0=1r_{0}=1, we set r^≡1\widehat{r}\equiv 1 (Assumption 3(i)). Under a shift, the base ratio is the classifier ratio of Sec. 3.2 with a logistic regression on (Z1,…,Z5)(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}), calibrated by Def. 2: for the ATE it balances g^\widehat{g} exactly, and for the CATE it balances g^2\widehat{g}^{2}, ζ​g^\zeta\widehat{g}, and ζk​ζl\zeta_{k}\zeta_{l} (k≤lk\leq l) within their standard errors δ^k\widehat{\delta}_{k} (Prop. 6). AIPWF uses ϵA=ϵB=10−3​Var^R​(Z0)\epsilon_{A}=\epsilon_{B}=10^{-3}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{R}(Z^{0}) in Eq. (11), and PPI++ fixes λ=0\lambda=0 and uses ω^=Proj[0,1]​(D^/B^)\widehat{\omega}=\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{D}/\widehat{B}), the rule of Angelopoulos et al. (2026) with our projection, without B^cal\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{cal}}. Shrinkage weights the naive pool by seR2/(seR2+gap2)\mathrm{se}_{R}^{2}/(\mathrm{se}_{R}^{2}+\mathrm{gap}^{2}), where gap\mathrm{gap} is the difference of the naive-pool and trial-only ATEs and seR\mathrm{se}_{R} is the trial-only standard error, and Pretest uses the naive pool when the gap is within 1.96​seR1.96\,\mathrm{se}_{R}. Shrinkage is a single-estimate rule in the spirit of Rosenman et al. (2023), not their Stein-type estimator, which shrinks the stratum estimates jointly. DRF and RF use the sieve ζ=(1,Z1,…,Z5,g^)\zeta=(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5},\widehat{g}), ridge ρ=0.01\rho=0.01, and the grid {0,0.5,1}2\{0,0.5,1\}^{2}, with ties broken toward smaller (λ,ω)(\lambda,\omega); their PPI++ versions use the grid points with λ=0\lambda=0. The trial-only learners use μ^R\widehat{\mu}_{R} and the sieve (1,Z1,…,Z5)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}) without g^\widehat{g}. 2-step fits g^+(1,Z1,…,Z5)⊤​β\widehat{g}+(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5})^{\top}\beta, with β\beta a ridge regression of the trial pseudo-outcome minus g^\widehat{g} (Kallus et al., 2018). IR (Wu and Yang, 2022) minimizes one RR-loss over the trial and OBS rows, in which the OBS rows add a bias function c⁡(x)c(x) to τ⁡(x)\tau(x). It takes τ\tau in (1,Z1,…,Z5)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}) and cc in (1,Z1O,…,Z5O,g^)(1,Z^{O}_{1},\dots,Z^{O}_{5},\widehat{g}), where ZkOZ^{O}_{k} are the principal components of the OBS nuisance covariates, and uses an OBS propensity from logistic regression. A ridge penalty replaces their SCAD penalty, and the penalty ratio λτ/λc∈{0,0.5,1,1.5}\lambda_{\tau}/\lambda_{c}\in\{0,0.5,1,1.5\} and λc∈{10−3,10−2,…,102}\lambda_{c}\in\{10^{-3},10^{-2},\dots,10^{2}\} are chosen by the RR-loss of both sources on the evaluation samples instead of cross-validation. The naive pool fits the same outcome regression to all trial and OBS rows, with no source indicator or weight and without clipping.

Metrics.

Each cell has 1,000 replications, seeded by the base seed 20261005, the design, the trial size, and the replication index, and no replication failed except 2 of the 10,000 misspecified-shift replications (IHDP, n=600n=600 and 3,0003{,}000), whose ratio calibration did not converge and which are left out. The ATE error is the estimate minus θ0\theta_{0}, and the CATE risk is 𝔼R​{τ^​(X)−τ0​(X)}2\mathbb{E}_{R}\{\hat{\tau}(X)-\tau_{0}(X)\}^{2} over 50,000 trial covariate draws (synthetic design) or all rows (benchmarks). The figures and Tables 5 and 6 report ratios of mean errors to the trial-only AIPW estimator or DR-learner; the figures add paired percentile 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the replications.

B.2 Bias and Observational Sample Size

Fig. 5 repeats the bias sweep at n=300n=300 and 900900. The ATE ratio of fusion is flat in the bias at every nn, and at n=3,000n=3{,}000 the CATE ratio of IR stays between 1.08 and 1.10 at every bias. The naive pool, Shrinkage, and Pretest beat fusion when the OBS are nearly unconfounded. At n=3,000n=3{,}000 the naive pool falls behind fusion at a bias between 0 and 0.25 (ATE) or between 0.25 and 0.5 (CATE) standard deviations. This threshold decreases as nn grows: for the CATE, it lies between 0.5 and 0.75 standard deviations at n=300n=300 and between 0.25 and 0.5 at n=3,000n=3{,}000. In Fig. 6, the ATE ratio of fusion changes little with NN, and its CATE ratio falls as NN grows. Fig. 8 gives the absolute errors.

B.3 Ablations and Further Designs

Patterns in Fig. 4.

The ATE gap of fusion below 1 is widest at small nn and narrows by n=3,000n=3{,}000, so the OBS help the ATE most when the trial is small; the CATE ratios of DRF and RF stay between 0.53 and 0.67 at every nn. PPI++ stays near 1 for the ATE and approaches DRF and RF for the CATE only at n=3,000n=3{,}000, so the gain of fusion at small nn comes from λ\lambda. For the ATE, this is the cap in Remark 1: the PPI correction can remove at most the share of effect heterogeneity in the score variance, which is small in these designs: at r0=1r_{0}=1, VarR​{τ0​(X)}/VarR​(Z0)\mathrm{Var}_{R}\{\tau_{0}(X)\}/\mathrm{Var}_{R}(Z^{0}) is 0.02 to 0.10 on the tuning samples. For the CATE, the trial-only learners use the sieve (1,Z1,…,Z5)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}) without g^\widehat{g}, whereas DRF, RF, and their PPI++ versions use (1,Z1,…,Z5,g^)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5},\widehat{g}), so the ratios to the trial-only learners combine the fusion loss with the gain from g^\widehat{g} as a basis function. The trial loss on the same sieve separates the two (Table 10): at large nn the gap comes from g^\widehat{g} as a basis function, and at small nn mostly from the fusion loss. IR, in contrast, reaches or exceeds the trial-only risk by n=3,000n=3{,}000 and is below it only on ACIC and on IHDP at n=300n=300. IR models the confounding function in a linear class, so the OBS rows inform τ\tau only as far as the OBS bias is close to that class. Its CATE class (1,Z1,…,Z5)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}) is the sieve of the trial-only learners, which is consistent with its ratio approaching or exceeding 1 as nn grows. DRF and RF do not model the confounding function, keep the trial’s target under any OBS confounding (Thm. 3), and use the OBS to reduce variance. The naive pool rises with nn, because its confounding bias stays fixed while the trial-only error shrinks. Shrinkage and Pretest never fall below 1 in columns 1–4.

Two channels.

Table 8 separates λ\lambda and ω\omega. At r0=1r_{0}=1, B^cal=0\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{cal}}=0, and fusion is at or below λ\lambda only in 14 of 15 cells, for example 0.55 against 0.60 on the synthetic design at n=300n=300. Under a shift, λ\lambda only is slightly below fusion in 28 of 30 cells, by at most 0.03, so once the ratio is estimated the PPI correction does not help in these designs. The rule ω^=Proj[0,1]​(D^/B^)\widehat{\omega}=\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{D}/\widehat{B}), which ignores B^cal\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{cal}}, does worse: Eq. (11) lowers the MSE of fusion by 1% to 4% in all 30 shift cells, and the old rule exceeds the trial-only MSE in three cells at n=3,000n=3{,}000 (1.01 to 1.04).

Practitioner’s baselines.

A practitioner without a tuning sample would use 3-fold cross-fitted trial-only AIPW and DR- and R-learners with the nuisances fitted on two thirds of the trial. This AIPW has lower MSE than the rotated trial-only AIPW of Table 5 in 42 of 45 cells (Table 9). Fusion is still below it in 42 of 45 cells; the exceptions are three shift cells at n=3,000n=3{,}000, at 1.00 to 1.01. DRF and RF are below the practitioner’s DR- and R-learners in all 45 cells, at 0.54 to 0.71 of their risk.

Same sieve.

Table 10 fits the trial loss alone on the sieve (1,Z1,…,Z5,g^)(1,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5},\widehat{g}), the grid point (λ,ω)=(0,0)(\lambda,\omega)=(0,0) of Algorithm 2. It uses g^\widehat{g}, so it is not a trial-only learner. It has 0.75 to 0.93 of the trial-only DR risk at n=300n=300 and 0.55 to 0.67 at n=3,000n=3{,}000. DRF and RF have 0.59 to 0.76 of its risk at n=300n=300 and 0.98 to 1.03 at n=3,000n=3{,}000. Thus at small nn most of the gain of DRF and RF over the trial-only learners comes from the fusion loss, and at large nn it comes from g^\widehat{g} as a basis function.

Misspecified ratio.

Table 11 uses a shift that the base ratio cannot represent. On the synthetic design and IHDP, the OBS tilts the trial law by exp⁡{a⁡(h2−1)/2}\exp\{a(h^{2}-1)/\sqrt{2}\} with a>0a>0 and effective sample fraction 0.40, so the OBS spread more widely along hh, while the logistic classifier on (Z1,…,Z5)(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{5}) is log-linear in hh. With the uncalibrated r^CLS\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CLS}}, for which ω^=Proj[0,1]​(D^/B^)\widehat{\omega}=\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{D}/\widehat{B}) and the standard error omits V^cal\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{cal}}, fusion is biased (0.08 to 0.12 on the synthetic design and 0.02 to 0.03 on IHDP), its coverage falls to 0.76 to 0.94, and its MSE exceeds the trial-only MSE at n≥900n\geq 900 (1.13 to 2.24). With r^BAL\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{BAL}}, the absolute bias is at most 0.005, the coverage is 0.94 to 0.96, and the MSE is 0.48 to 0.99 of the trial-only MSE. DRF and RF have 0.52 to 0.62 of the trial-only CATE risk here.

Large heterogeneity.

Table 12 changes the synthetic design so that ω\omega can matter: the outcome noise is 0.2 instead of 0.7, VarR​τ0​(X)=5.88\mathrm{Var}_{R}\tau_{0}(X)=5.88 instead of 1.47, and ν0\nu_{0} is unchanged, so the confounding bias is 0.75​sdR​τ0​(X)0.75\,\mathrm{sd}_{R}\tau_{0}(X). The heterogeneity share VarR​{τ0​(X)}/VarR​(Z0)\mathrm{Var}_{R}\{\tau_{0}(X)\}/\mathrm{Var}_{R}(Z^{0}) rises to 0.20 to 0.33. At r0=1r_{0}=1, PPI++ has 0.83 to 0.93 of the trial-only MSE, and fusion improves on λ\lambda only at every nn, from 0.60 to 0.45 at n=300n=300 and from 0.96 to 0.89 at n=3,000n=3{,}000. Under the strong shift, PPI++ is above 1 (1.07 to 1.30), and fusion is above λ\lambda only (0.62 against 0.60 at n=300n=300, 1.06 against 0.96 at n=3,000n=3{,}000). Eq. (11) reduces this loss relative to the rule ω^=Proj[0,1]​(D^/B^)\widehat{\omega}=\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{D}/\widehat{B}) (0.66 and 1.26) but does not remove it. The coverage of fusion is 0.95 to 0.96 throughout. The prognostic-score adjustments do worse here: Prog. score has 1.38 to 2.24 of the trial-only MSE, and Cov. + prog. score has 0.73 at n=300n=300 and 1.03 to 1.20 for n≥900n\geq 900, against 0.45 to 1.06 for fusion.

B.4 Comparison with Prognostic-Score Adjustment

Estimators.

Prog. score is the least-squares fit of YY on (1,A,s,A​s)(1,A,s,As) over the whole trial, where ss is μ^O​(X,0)\widehat{\mu}_{O}(X,0) centered on the trial, and Cov. + prog. score is the least-squares fit of YY on (1,A,X,μ^O​(X,0))(1,A,X,\widehat{\mu}_{O}(X,0)). Both use the μ^O\widehat{\mu}_{O} of fusion, report the coefficient of AA with a sandwich standard error, and keep the trial’s target under any OBS confounding because the trial is randomized. They are the linear prognostic-score adjustment of Schuler et al. (2022); Liao et al. (2025) and Højbjerre-Frandsen et al. (2026) put the same score into efficient and GLM plug-in estimators. All of them target the ATE; none of them estimates the CATE.

Results.

Table 13 and Fig. 7 compare them with fusion on the 45 settings of Sec. 5. On IHDP they match fusion, and Prog. score is slightly better at n=300n=300 under a shift (0.45 against 0.47 and 0.48). On ACIC, fusion is at or below both adjustments in 14 of 15 settings. On the synthetic design, Prog. score exceeds the trial-only MSE for n≥600n\geq 600 (up to 1.50), and Cov. + prog. score exceeds it at n=3,000n=3{,}000. Over the 45 settings, fusion is at or below both adjustments in 35, and the paired 95% bootstrap interval of the MSE ratio of fusion to the better adjustment is below 1 in 16 settings and above 1 in 2. Fusion never exceeds the trial-only MSE. The coverage of the 95% Wald intervals is 0.94 to 0.96 for fusion and Prog. score and 0.91 to 0.97 for Cov. + prog. score. Under large effect heterogeneity (Table 12), Prog. score has 1.38 to 2.24 of the trial-only MSE and Cov. + prog. score 0.73 to 1.20, against 0.45 to 1.06 for fusion. For the CATE, the closest analogue is the trial loss on the sieve with g^\widehat{g} (Table 10), which uses the OBS prediction only as a basis function.
